title: Endocrine glands and their hormones
blurb: Match each endocrine gland to its hormones and actions, tell steroid from peptide hormones, and recognize the classic hormone disorders.
question: A patient produces large volumes of very dilute urine and is constantly thirsty, yet his blood glucose is normal. Which hormone is most likely deficient, which structure makes it, and which structure releases it?

teach.body: Formally, the endocrine system is a set of ductless glands that release hormones into the blood; each hormone acts only on target cells that carry matching receptors. In plain English: hormones are letters mailed through the bloodstream, and only cells with the right mailbox can read them. Exocrine glands, by contrast, use ducts (sweat and salivary glands). The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems, and most hormone levels are held steady by negative feedback.

teach.caption: Thyroid hormones (T3, T4) are amines that act like steroids: they bind intracellular receptors.

root.label: Hypothalamus
root.sub: Releasing hormones; makes ADH and oxytocin

teach.caption: The hypothalamus sends releasing and inhibiting hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH) to the anterior pituitary.

head: Gland
Hormone
Main action
rows: Raise metabolic rate and heat; need iodine
teach.caption: Ovaries make estrogen and progesterone; testes make testosterone. Delta cells of the pancreas make somatostatin, which inhibits insulin and glucagon.
Aldosterone makes the kidneys reabsorb Na+ (water follows) and excrete K+. Cortisol raises blood glucose and suppresses inflammation and immunity.

teach.body: The posterior pituitary is a storage depot, not a factory: ADH and oxytocin are made by the hypothalamus and travel down to the posterior pituitary, which releases them. ADH (vasopressin) makes the kidney collecting ducts reabsorb water, so urine becomes smaller in volume and more concentrated. Oxytocin drives uterine contractions in labor and milk ejection, while prolactin from the anterior pituitary drives milk production.

head: Disorder
Cause
rows: Autoimmune loss of beta cells: no insulin
ADH deficiency: lots of dilute urine; not a glucose problem
Excess T3/T4: weight loss, heat intolerance, fast HR
Low T3/T4: weight gain, cold intolerance, fatigue
Excess GH before / after growth plates close

teach.body: Mr. Hughes passes large volumes of pale, dilute urine and is always thirsty, but his blood glucose is normal, which rules out diabetes mellitus. His team suspects diabetes insipidus: too little ADH. ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. Without it, the collecting ducts reabsorb less water, so water is lost in the urine. Despite the shared word 'diabetes', the problem is water balance, not blood sugar.

teach.text: Swaps that cost points: the hypothalamus MAKES ADH and oxytocin, the posterior pituitary releases them. Epinephrine comes from the adrenal MEDULLA, cortisol from the CORTEX. Calcitonin lowers Ca2+, PTH raises it. Thyroid hormones need iodine, not calcium. Melatonin is from the pineal gland. Steroids bind receptors INSIDE the cell. Endocrine glands are ductless.

items: Endocrine glands are ductless and secrete hormones into the blood; only cells with matching receptors respond.
Steroid hormones (from cholesterol) bind intracellular receptors; peptide hormones bind membrane receptors and use second messengers.
Anterior pituitary: GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin. Posterior pituitary releases hypothalamic ADH and oxytocin.
Thyroid: T3/T4 (iodine), calcitonin. Parathyroids: PTH. Pancreas: insulin (beta), glucagon (alpha). Pineal: melatonin.
Adrenal cortex: aldosterone and cortisol. Adrenal medulla: epinephrine and norepinephrine.

summary: You can now match each endocrine gland to its hormones and actions, explain how steroid and peptide hormones reach their receptors, and separate what the hypothalamus makes from what the pituitary releases. You can also recognize the classic disorders from their hormone cause.

A.q: Which gland secretes melatonin, the hormone that regulates the sleep-wake cycle?
A.why: The pineal gland secretes melatonin, which rises in darkness and sets the circadian rhythm.

whyNot.0: The anterior pituitary secretes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin, not melatonin.
whyNot.1: The thymus secretes thymosin for T-cell maturation.
whyNot.3: The hypothalamus regulates sleep cycles and controls the pituitary, but it does not secrete melatonin.

A.q: Which hormone is made by the hypothalamus but stored and released by the posterior pituitary?
A.why: ADH (and oxytocin) are made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary.

whyNot.1: Prolactin is made and released by the anterior pituitary.
whyNot.2: Growth hormone comes from the anterior pituitary.
whyNot.3: TSH is made and released by the anterior pituitary.

A.q: How do steroid hormones such as cortisol act on their target cells?
options: By binding receptors on the cell surface
By binding receptors inside the cell
By activating cAMP at the membrane
By traveling to targets through ducts
A.why: Steroids are lipid-soluble, cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors, changing gene expression.

whyNot.0: Surface (membrane) receptors are used by water-soluble peptide hormones such as insulin.
whyNot.2: cAMP is the second messenger used by peptide hormones that bind membrane receptors.
whyNot.3: Endocrine glands are ductless; hormones travel in the blood.

B.q: Which pair of hormones does the adrenal medulla secrete?
B.why: The adrenal medulla (inner) secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine for the short-term, fight-or-flight stress response.

whyNot.0: Cortisol and aldosterone both come from the adrenal cortex, not the medulla.
whyNot.1: Aldosterone is a cortex hormone, so this pair mixes the two regions.
whyNot.2: Cortisol is a cortex hormone, so this pair mixes the two regions.

B.q: Production of T3 and T4 by the thyroid depends on an adequate dietary supply of which element?
B.why: Thyroid hormones contain iodine; iodine deficiency reduces T3/T4 and can cause a goiter.

whyNot.0: Calcium is regulated by PTH and calcitonin but is not part of T3 or T4.
whyNot.1: Iron is needed for hemoglobin, not thyroid hormones.
whyNot.3: Sodium balance is regulated by aldosterone; it is not built into thyroid hormones.

B.q: Which gland secretes parathyroid hormone (PTH), and what is its effect?
B.why: The four parathyroid glands secrete PTH, which raises blood calcium by releasing bone calcium, conserving it in the kidneys and activating vitamin D.

whyNot.1: Lowering blood calcium is the job of calcitonin, PTH's opposite.
whyNot.2: The thyroid secretes calcitonin, which lowers calcium; PTH comes from the parathyroids.
whyNot.3: The adrenal cortex secretes aldosterone and cortisol, not PTH.

C.q: A patient has extreme thirst and passes large volumes of very dilute urine. His fasting blood glucose is normal. Which condition is most likely?
C.why: Dilute, high-volume urine with normal glucose points to diabetes insipidus, a lack of ADH (or kidney insensitivity to it).

whyNot.0: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (no insulin) would raise blood glucose.
whyNot.1: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (insulin resistance) would also raise blood glucose.
whyNot.3: Addison's disease is low cortisol and aldosterone, not a lack of ADH.

C.q: Cushing's syndrome is caused by an excess of which hormone, produced by which region of the adrenal gland?
C.why: Cushing's syndrome is excess cortisol, a glucocorticoid made by the adrenal cortex.

whyNot.0: Cortisol is correct but it comes from the cortex; the medulla makes epinephrine and norepinephrine.
whyNot.1: Epinephrine is made by the adrenal medulla and is not the cause of Cushing's.
whyNot.2: Aldosterone is a cortex hormone, and Cushing's is a cortisol excess.

C.q: Which statement about the anterior pituitary is correct?
options: It releases TSH, which stimulates the thyroid
It makes ADH and oxytocin, then releases them
It secretes calcitonin to lower blood calcium
It releases ACTH to stimulate the adrenal medulla
C.why: The anterior pituitary secretes TSH, which stimulates the thyroid to produce T3 and T4.

whyNot.1: ADH and oxytocin are made by the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary.
whyNot.2: Calcitonin comes from the thyroid's C cells, not the pituitary.
whyNot.3: ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex (cortisol), not the medulla.

reteach.title: A head office and its branches
reteach.question: Picture a company with a head office, a manager who passes on head-office orders, and branch offices that each make one product. Where does each endocrine gland fit?

blocks.body: The hypothalamus is the head office: it writes the orders (releasing hormones) and even prepares two finished products itself (ADH and oxytocin), which it ships to a warehouse, the posterior pituitary, for dispatch. The anterior pituitary is the regional manager: it receives head-office orders and sends its own memos (TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH) to the branch offices. The branches (thyroid, adrenal cortex, gonads) then make their products: T3/T4, cortisol, sex hormones.

blocks.text: The warehouse (posterior pituitary) only ships ADH and oxytocin; it does not make them. The head office (hypothalamus) does.

explain.body: Endocrine glands are ductless and secrete hormones into the blood. Steroid hormones bind receptors inside cells; peptide hormones bind membrane receptors.

test.q: Which feature defines an endocrine gland?
options: It releases its product through a duct
It signals targets by nerve impulses
It releases hormones directly into blood
It secretes onto a body surface or lumen
test.why: Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into the blood.

whyNot.0: Releasing through a duct is the defining feature of exocrine glands.
whyNot.1: Nerve impulses are nervous-system signaling; hormones travel in the blood.
whyNot.3: Secreting onto a surface or into a lumen is exocrine secretion.

explain.body: The anterior pituitary makes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and prolactin. The posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin, which the hypothalamus makes.

rows.label: Hormones
values: GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, PRL

test.q: Which hormone is released by the posterior pituitary to trigger milk ejection during breastfeeding?
test.why: Oxytocin, released by the posterior pituitary, causes milk ejection and uterine contractions.

whyNot.0: Prolactin drives milk production, and it comes from the anterior pituitary.
whyNot.2: Growth hormone comes from the anterior pituitary and drives growth.
whyNot.3: LH is an anterior pituitary gonadotropin acting on the gonads.

explain.body: Thyroid: T3/T4 and calcitonin. Parathyroids: PTH. Pancreas: insulin and glucagon. Pineal: melatonin. Thymus: thymosin. Kidneys: EPO. Heart: ANP.

test.q: What is the main action of thymosin, secreted by the thymus?
test.why: Thymosin promotes the maturation of T cells; the thymus is large in children and shrinks with age.

whyNot.0: The sleep-wake rhythm is set by melatonin from the pineal gland.
whyNot.2: Red blood cell production is stimulated by erythropoietin from the kidneys.
whyNot.3: Lowering blood volume and BP is the action of ANP from the heart's atria.

explain.body: The cortex makes aldosterone (Na+ in, K+ out) and cortisol (long-term stress, raises glucose). The medulla makes epinephrine and norepinephrine for short-term fight or flight.

test.q: What does aldosterone cause the kidneys to do?
test.why: Aldosterone makes the kidneys reabsorb Na+ (water follows) and excrete K+, raising blood volume and BP.

whyNot.0: The ions are reversed: aldosterone retains Na+ and excretes K+.
whyNot.1: Inserting aquaporins to reabsorb water is the action of ADH.
whyNot.2: Excreting Na+ and water is the action of ANP, aldosterone's opposite.
